analysis.one_liner: Repeals oil and gas company tax breaks and refunds the revenue to registered vehicle owners.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and sat there until the 112th Congress ended, despite 17 Democratic cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would end several federal tax breaks for oil and gas companies — including credits for enhanced oil recovery and marginal wells, the expensing of drilling costs, and percentage depletion — and deny them the domestic manufacturing tax deduction. It would then divide the resulting revenue among every registered vehicle owner as an income tax rebate, paid per vehicle. It was introduced in March 2012 and referred to the Ways and Means Committee, where it died without a hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Registered owners of cars, trucks, and other motor vehicles in the United States, who would receive a rebate against their income tax for each vehicle they own; the rebate would be funded entirely by the revenue raised from repealing the oil and gas tax preferences.

how_it_helps.text: Each registered vehicle owner would receive a rebate equal to the revenue raised by the repeal of the oil and gas tax breaks divided by the total number of registered vehicles, multiplied by the number of vehicles they own [S3].
The rebate would be treated as a payment against income tax and refunded or credited as rapidly as possible, with no interest [S3].
Low-income households that spend a larger share of their budget on gasoline would get relief tied directly to the tax breaks that subsidize oil companies [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies, which would lose the enhanced oil recovery credit, the marginal well credit, expensing of intangible drilling and development costs, the tertiary injectant deduction, the passive-loss exception for working interests, percentage depletion, and the domestic production deduction [S2].

drawbacks.text: The rebate is divided per vehicle, so households with several cars would receive several rebates, and people who do not own a registered vehicle — including many low-income renters — would get nothing even though they pay fuel costs indirectly [S3].

The oil industry's standard argument is that these provisions encourage domestic drilling and production, so repealing them could modestly reduce domestic output and put upward pressure on fuel prices; an honest supporter would acknowledge some price risk [S2].

The rebate amount depends on a ten-year revenue estimate by the Treasury Secretary, so the payment is inherently uncertain and would be a one-time credit in the year of enactment rather than an ongoing benefit [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design is straightforward: the same revenue is taken from oil company tax preferences and handed back to drivers. The main fairness gap is that the rebate reaches vehicle owners only and scales with the number of vehicles, so the poorest households — who often do not own a car yet pay energy costs indirectly — are missed, while multi-car owners do best. On the other side, some of the repealed provisions do support domestic production, so a small fuel-price effect cannot be ruled out. Overall the benefits to drivers outweigh those costs, but the bill never got far enough for any of this to be tested.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up, so it died there when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Rep. John Yarmuth introduced the Gas Rebate Act of 2012 on March 21, 2012, with 13 original cosponsors, all Democrats [S1],[S3].
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day; no further action was ever taken on the bill [S5].
The bill ended the Congress with 17 cosponsors, all Democrats, and never received a committee markup, hearing, or floor vote [S4],[S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies kept all the tax preferences the bill would have repealed, and drivers never received the rebate. The Ways and Means Committee's inaction was enough to end the proposal, since no bill can reach the House floor without a committee clearing it or a rare procedural maneuver.

for.name: Rep. John Yarmuth
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 17 cosponsors for it.

for.name: 17 House Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including 13 original cosponsors named at introduction such as Reps. Connolly, Conyers, Stark, Van Hollen, and Rangel.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral with jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral on March 21, 2012, without a hearing, markup, or vote, for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Rep. Dave Camp
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee consideration during his chairmanship.

sides.party_line_note: All 17 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on; with Republicans holding the House majority and the Ways and Means chairmanship, the bill never advanced.

industries.note: The bill would repeal six specific tax preferences plus the domestic production deduction for oil and gas activities, directly costing the industry revenue it currently receives under the tax code [S2],[S3]. Drivers would be repaid out of that same revenue, so the industry's loss is the public's gain under this bill [S3].

industries.industry: Marginal and small independent well operators
industries.note: The marginal well credit and percentage depletion are used disproportionately by smaller producers of high-cost wells; repealing them would hit this segment hardest, though the bill'sframers treat that revenue as the source of the driver rebate [S2],[S3].
